---
title: "Biological Execution Model"
---

## Why tensors are not enough

A tensor describes shape, storage, strides, dtype, and device. That is insufficient for Cellerator.

A dimension of length 20,000 might contain:

- canonical genes;
- packed genes;
- a different gene panel;
- regulatory elements;
- motif occurrences;
- latent channels;
- one partition of a larger domain.

Two arrays can have identical dimensions and incompatible biological meaning.

Cellerator therefore needs a model in which biological identity is explicit and computationally active.

## Domains

A biological domain is an ordered set or coordinate space of entities.

Examples include:

- genomic coordinates;
- motif occurrences;
- regulatory elements;
- genes;
- transcripts;
- proteins;
- cells;
- developmental states;
- pathways;
- regulatory modules;
- latent dimensions.

```cpp
enum class domain_kind : std::uint32_t {
    sequence_coordinate,
    motif_occurrence,
    regulatory_element,
    gene,
    transcript,
    protein,
    cell,
    developmental_state,
    module,
    pathway,
    latent,
    user_defined
};

struct domain_descriptor {
    domain_id identity;
    domain_kind kind;

    std::uint64_t logical_size;
    order_id canonical_order;

    domain_encoding encoding;
    metadata_handle metadata;
};
```

A sequence-coordinate domain may be implicit and contiguous. A gene domain may be an explicit table. A latent domain may be model-defined.

The core should not encode every ontology. It should provide stable identity and enough kind information for validation and dispatch.

## Axis identity

Every biologically meaningful operand axis carries:

```cpp
struct axis_identity {
    domain_id domain;
    order_id order;
    geometry_id geometry;
    partition_id partition;
};
```

The fields mean:

- `domain`: which entities are present;
- `order`: their exact permutation;
- `geometry`: how they are grouped or tiled;
- `partition`: which subset and ownership view is present.

`geometry` may be null when grouping is irrelevant. `partition` may represent the complete domain.

Persistent identities should be strong hashes or UUID-like values. A loaded execution session may intern them into compact handles.

## Relations

A typed relation connects two or more domains.

```cpp
struct relation_descriptor {
    relation_id identity;
    relation_semantics semantics;

    domain_id source;
    domain_id destination;

    structure_id structure;
};
```

Examples:

```text
sequence coordinate → motif occurrence
motif occurrence → regulatory element
regulatory element → gene
gene → transcript
protein → pathway
cell → expressed gene
cell → active module
module → latent channel
cell → neighboring cell
```

A relation is not required to be represented as a matrix. A matrix is one mathematical view over a binary relation with values.

## Structures and value planes

A structure defines topology:

- which edges exist;
- which entities are grouped;
- which order is used;
- which physical projections are available.

A value plane supplies numbers or logical state over that structure.

```cpp
struct relation_structure {
    structure_id identity;
    std::uint64_t structure_epoch;

    relation_descriptor relation;
    projection_catalog projections;
};

struct value_plane {
    const relation_structure* structure;

    const void* values;
    dtype storage_type;
    dtype logical_type;

    quantization_descriptor quantization;

    std::uint64_t value_generation;
    value_layout layout;
};
```

Examples:

- one enhancer-to-gene structure with cell-specific edge weights;
- one gene-regulatory structure with learned values;
- one cell-by-gene support structure with expression values at many time points;
- one motif-to-element structure with Boolean, count, or affinity planes;
- one sparse topology with fp16 execution values and fp32 master values.

## Operand plurality

Cellerator should not force every biological object into a dense tensor or conventional sparse matrix.

```cpp
enum class operand_kind : std::uint32_t {
    dense_tensor,
    bit_plane,
    event_stream,
    segment_stream,
    sparse_relation,
    scalar_parameter
};

struct biological_operand_view {
    operand_kind kind;
    axis_identity axes[max_operand_rank];
    device_id device;

    union {
        dense_tensor_view dense;
        bit_plane_view bits;
        event_stream_view events;
        segment_stream_view segments;
        sparse_relation_view relation;
        scalar_parameter_view scalar;
    };
};
```

Each representation retains its natural compact form.

A planner may choose to materialize or transform it when the next operation benefits.

## Sequence and level

Sequence and quantitative level are not alien datatypes.

Sequence is usually:

- immutable;
- coordinate-indexed;
- compact;
- Boolean or low-bit;
- transformed by exact predicates.

Level is usually:

- dynamic;
- associated with genes, transcripts, proteins, cells, modules, or edges;
- integer, fixed-point, or floating point;
- transformed by weighted propagation and state updates.

Both are value planes over domains or relations.

The complete path can remain inside one model:

```text
sequence coordinate domain
    ↓ exact predicate
motif mask or motif occurrence domain
    ↓ interval or grammar relation
regulatory element domain
    ↓ accessibility and TF activity
active regulatory relation
    ↓ element-to-gene propagation
gene domain
    ↓ transcription and degradation
transcript level
    ↓ translation and interaction
protein and pathway state
    ↓ cell or tissue model
phenotype and behavior
```

The representation changes only when the operation changes its mathematical nature.

## The numerical border

Keep the computation Boolean or integer through:

- nucleotide identity;
- validity;
- motif matching;
- strand;
- spacing grammar;
- coordinate ownership;
- interval membership;
- support masks;
- compact counts.

Convert to floating point at the first genuinely quantitative interaction, such as:

- binding affinity;
- TF activity;
- chromatin-weighted occupancy;
- enhancer strength;
- learned regulatory weight;
- transcriptional drive;
- kinetic state.

There is no single global numerical border. The planner may place it differently for different operations.

## Example: static DNA with dynamic cell state

Static sequence work should usually be amortized.

```text
packed genome
    ↓ once
Baseplane motif and grammar program
    ↓ once
motif-to-regulatory-element structure
    ↓ once
CellPack semantic geometry and projections
    ↓ repeated
cell-specific accessibility and TF value planes
    ↓ repeated
regulatory propagation and expression update
```

The immutable sequence program and regulatory topology can serve millions of cell-state evaluations.

## Execution order

An order is a first-class property of every axis.

```cpp
struct tensor_view {
    void* data;
    dtype type;
    shape shape;
    stride stride;
    axis_identity axes[max_rank];
    std::uint64_t value_generation;
    device_id device;
};
```

### Producer and consumer contracts

A kernel declares:

- accepted source domains;
- accepted input orders;
- required geometry;
- produced order;
- whether it can fuse an order transform;
- whether it preserves partition ownership.

```cpp
struct axis_requirement {
    domain_constraint domain;
    order_constraint order;
    geometry_constraint geometry;
    partition_constraint partition;
};

struct kernel_contract {
    axis_requirement inputs[max_inputs][max_rank];
    produced_axis outputs[max_outputs][max_rank];
};
```

### Graph-wide order optimization

For graph node \(i\) and candidate order \(q_i\), minimize:

\[
\sum_i C_{\text{kernel}}(i, q_i)
+
\sum_{(i,j)}
C_{\text{transform}}(q_i, q_j)
\]

This prevents a locally fast kernel from winning when it forces expensive gather and scatter operations around itself.

Order transforms may be:

- removed through producer-consumer agreement;
- fused into a kernel;
- hoisted to graph entry;
- delayed to graph exit;
- cached by source allocation and value generation;
- represented as metadata when access remains valid without movement.

## Hierarchy

Biological hierarchy is a set of overlapping relations and partitions.

A strict tree is usually wrong.

A gene may belong to several pathways. An enhancer may contact several genes. A regulatory module may overlap another module. A cell may occupy several continuous state coordinates.

Represent hierarchy through:

- membership relations;
- parent-child relations;
- nested partitions;
- overlapping views;
- optional compiler priors.

Do not duplicate the underlying values for every hierarchy.

## Module-local dense state

The transition from sparse biological input to learned dense state can preserve locality.

Instead of immediately producing:

```text
[cell][unstructured hidden dimension]
```

a native first learned layer can produce:

```text
[cell tile][biological module][local hidden channel]
```

This permits:

- module-local MLPs;
- grouped linear operations;
- conditional module execution;
- module-specific normalization;
- local quantization;
- sparse cross-module communication;
- later controlled collapse into global latent state.

## Conditional execution

A hierarchy may support exact or approximate skipping.

Exact skipping is safe when:

- a module activity mask is zero;
- a required regulatory gate is false;
- a sequence predicate produces no relevant relation;
- all values in a module are structurally absent.

Approximate skipping requires an explicit error policy and validation.

A route decision selects precompiled work. It must not assemble new modules in the hot path.

## State transitions

Many biological processes are naturally sparse state updates.

A generic regulatory update may be:

\[
d_{c,g}
=
b_g
+
\sum_e L_{e,g} o_{c,e}
\]

\[
RNA_{c,g}^{t+\Delta t}
=
RNA_{c,g}^{t}
+
\Delta t
\left[
s_g(d_{c,g})
-
\lambda_g RNA_{c,g}^{t}
\right]
\]

The same fixed relation structure can be reused across time steps. Only value planes change.

This makes recurrent, trajectory, Jacobian-vector, and graph-propagation operations natural Cellerator primitives.

## Sparse programs

A biological sparse program is a graph of typed operations over domains and relations.

Possible operations include:

- predicate;
- join;
- gather or scatter;
- masked weighted propagation;
- segmented reduction;
- module reduction;
- sparse-dense projection;
- gating;
- normalization;
- nonlinear state update;
- top-k event selection;
- neighborhood aggregation;
- communication;
- order transform.

The program can be compiled into:

- selected semantic geometries;
- physical projections;
- fused kernels;
- graph replay;
- communication schedules.

The initial implementation should remain a compact POD-oriented runtime rather than a large dynamic compiler framework. The semantic model should nevertheless guide every ABI added now.

## Identity failure modes

The runtime must reject:

- same shape, different domain;
- same domain, different order;
- same order, stale geometry;
- same structure identity, changed topology;
- same values pointer, stale value generation;
- incompatible partition ownership;
- sequence event streams from the wrong coordinate domain;
- relations whose source and destination domains do not match the consumer.

Identity checks may be compiled down or interned for hot execution after preparation. They must remain available at boundaries and in validation builds.

## Design outcome

The unified space is not one giant tensor.

It is a connected system of domains, relations, structures, values, and orders whose natural physical representations remain intact until a measured operation benefits from changing them.

That is how sequence and level become parts of one execution model without paying for an artificial universal representation.
